en: Petavatthu, Uragavagga, 7. The Story of the Peti Who Ate Seven Sons [The Buddha said: "Once upon a time, monks, there was a certain brahmin woman who lived in Benares. She was poor, destitute, and without means of subsistence. Having no other way to provide for herself, she went from house to house begging for alms. At that time, a certain man had seven sons. When they were old enough to play, they would go out to play together. One day, as they were playing outside the city, they saw a peta standing at the city gate. He was extremely emaciated, with veins protruding all over his body, and he was suffering greatly from hunger and thirst. Seeing him, the boys asked: 'Who are you, sir? 'I am a peta,' he replied. 'What did you do in your previous life to become such a being? 'I was a human being, but I committed evil deeds; therefore, I have been reborn here in the realm of petas. 'What evil deed did you commit? 'I was a man who ate the flesh of his own sons. [The Buddha continued: "Monks, what do you think? That man who ate the flesh of his own sons—was he anyone else? It was none other than this very peta. Because of that evil deed, he suffered for many hundreds of thousands of years in the realms of hell, and even now, as a peta, he continues to suffer from hunger and thirst. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall not take life, nor shall we eat the flesh of our own sons. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves."
“Naked you are, of ugly form,
foul-smelling and emitting stench;
you are surrounded by flies.”
“Who are you that stands here?
“Venerable sir, I am a female peta,
miserable, belonging to the world of Yama.”
Having committed evil deeds,
they have gone from here to the world of the departed.
In due course, seven sons...
In the evening seven more;
having given birth, I devour them,
yet even they are not enough for me.
It burns and smokes;
my heart is consumed by hunger;
I find no peace.
“As if burnt by fire in the heat.
“What evil deed has been committed by body, speech, or mind?”
“By the ripening of what karma do you eat the flesh of your own sons?
“I had two sons,” he replied.
Both of us having reached the prime of youth,
and endowed with the strength of sons,
I held my husband in contempt.
Then my husband, being angry,
brought a rival wife to me;
she conceived a child.
I conceived an evil thought toward her.
With a corrupted mind,
I brought about her miscarriage.
Her three-month-old fetus fell out as putrid blood;
her mother became angry at this.
He brought my kinsmen together;
he made me take an oath and caused me to be reviled.
I uttered a terrible oath and spoke a falsehood:
“I am eating the flesh of my own son.”
If that was indeed done by me—
by the ripening of that karma,
of both that false speech and this [other deed].
“I eat the flesh of my sons, smeared with pus and blood. The seventh account:
The Story of Her Who Caused Her Seven Sons to Be Eaten.
